paras: The expulsion of George Brown from Salem, Nebraska, took place in April 1903, when residents of the town, acting through a citizens' meeting, forced Brown, a Black man from Falls City, to give up a house he had rented there and leave. Brown left after a committee ordered him out, and the dispatches noted that Salem had never had a Black resident. Editors in Iowa, Mississippi and Georgia used the episode to charge Northern Republicans with hypocrisy on race.

Brown, described in an Omaha dispatch as "a respectable negro" of Falls City, decided several days before April 21 to move to Salem, which the dispatch called "a town in the next county." He went to Salem and rented a house. Accounts differ on how far the move had gone: the Omaha dispatch said he had moved his family into the house, while two reports datelined Salem said he had rented it "preparatory to moving his family in" or had "signified his intention" of bringing them. All three reports stated that no Black person had ever lived in Salem.

According to the Omaha dispatch, a mass meeting was held the evening after Brown moved in, and it was decided that, because no Black person had ever lived in Salem, he would not be allowed to stay. That report attributed the action to "an organization of business men" and said a committee called on Brown and ordered him to leave at once. Brown at first refused but later agreed and left town on April 21; the dispatch added, "The arguments used to him cannot be discovered."

A Salem special to the Norfolk News gave a briefer version, in which a public meeting of citizens "served a warning on him to stay away" and residents held it "an unwritten law" that no Black person should ever live there. A second Salem dispatch, dated April 22, said only that after a meeting of citizens Brown "was compelled to leave."
No report of arrests, legal action or any official response appears in the coverage, and none of the reports gives Brown's own account or says where his family went.

The story circulated in white newspapers as short dispatches, and no Black newspaper account of it appears in the coverage. The April 22 Salem wire, headed "Salem Has a Prejudice," ran the same day in the Beatrice Daily Express, on April 23 in the Denison Review in Iowa, on April 24 in the Norfolk Weekly News-Journal, and on April 25 in the Baxter Springs News in Kansas as "No Negroes at Salem, Neb." The Norfolk paper also printed its own Salem special under the head "Negroes Not Wanted," without comment.

In Mississippi, the Hattiesburg Daily Progress ran the Omaha version as "People of Nebraska Order Negro to Leave Town," opening with the line that "Republican Nebraska has no more use for the negro than the democratic south." The Missouri Valley Times in Iowa, using a slur for Brown, remarked that had the episode occurred in Louisiana, President Roosevelt "would have closed up the post office" and Nebraska's Republican papers would have approved. In May the Marietta Journal in Georgia printed an editorial credited to the American Press, "Nebraska Hard on Negroes," which did not name Brown but said he and his family "had a perfect right to locate in Salem" and called the affair "the same old story of Northern hatred for negroes." The Dawson News in Georgia reprinted the editorial's account of the meeting later that month.

accounts.label: Omaha dispatch
accounts.gist: Brown moved his family into a rented house; a mass meeting the next evening resolved he could not stay; a committee of a business men's organization ordered him out, and after first refusing he left on April 21.

accounts.label: Salem special to the Norfolk News
accounts.gist: Brown rented a house preparatory to moving his family in; a public meeting served a warning on him to stay away, under an 'unwritten law' that no Black person should live there.

accounts.label: Salem wire, April 22
accounts.gist: Brown rented a house and signified his intention of moving his family; after a citizens' meeting he was compelled to leave.

accounts.label: Southern editorial (American Press)
accounts.gist: An unnamed Black man contemplating residence was warned by a 'mass indignation meeting' and abandoned his plan.

framing.detail: Nebraska, Iowa and Kansas papers ran the short Salem wire under 'Salem Has a Prejudice' or 'No Negroes at Salem, Neb.' without comment.
The Norfolk paper's own special, 'Negroes Not Wanted', reported the 'unwritten law' without comment.

The Mississippi paper's Omaha dispatch, 'People of Nebraska Order Negro to Leave Town', opened with a partisan jab that 'Republican Nebraska' had no more use for Black people than the 'democratic south'.
The Missouri Valley Times used a slur and mocked Roosevelt and Nebraska Republican papers, ridiculing the 'poor colored man' sentiment rather than condemning Salem.
The Georgia editorial 'Nebraska Hard on Negroes' said the family had 'a perfect right' to live there and called it Northern hatred and hypocrisy.
